passages.text: COAL, or PIT-COAL, a black inflammable fossil, dug out of the earth in beds or seams, and much used for fuel.

Naturalists are divided about its origin. Some hold it to be a mineral bitumen, which, having penetrated a stratum of earth, has hardened with it into a stone; others think it is formed of trees and other vegetables, buried in the earth and changed by length of time.
In favour of the last opinion it is observed, that the slate or shale which lies above the coal often bears the impressions of ferns and other plants.
The beds of coal, with the strata of stone between them, are supposed by many to have been laid down by the waters of the deluge, which tore up the forests of the old world and buried them.
Coal is found in great plenty in Britain, chiefly about Newcastle, in Scotland, and in Wales; and the stock is so great that it may be thought inexhaustible.
The miners are much exposed to an inflammable vapour called fire-damp, which, taking fire from their candles, explodes with great violence, and often kills many of them.
Pit-coal yields, by distillation, a tar, an oil, and a volatile alkali; and what remains is called coke, which is now used for smelting iron.
Coal is a combustible black or brownish-black sedimentary rock, formed as rock strata called coal seams. It is mostly carbon, with variable amounts of hydrogen, sulfur, oxygen and nitrogen.
Coal forms when dead plant matter decays into peat and is converted into coal by the heat and pressure of deep burial over millions of years.
Many large coal deposits come from wetland forests that grew during the Carboniferous and Permian periods, hundreds of millions of years ago.
Fossils of plants, such as ferns and giant club mosses, are common in the shale beds that lie with coal seams.
British coal output reached its peak in 1913 and then declined. Most British coal mines are now closed, and the last coal-fired power station in the United Kingdom closed in 2024.
Firedamp, a gas that is mostly methane, collects in coal mines and can explode when it meets a flame. Such explosions have killed many miners.
Coke, made by heating coal without air, is used to smelt iron ore in blast furnaces. Coal tar is a by-product of making coke.
Burning coal releases carbon dioxide. Coal is the largest single source of the carbon dioxide emissions that cause climate change.

reasons: Rare terms appear in both: seams, shale, ferns, fire-damp, coke.
Coal mining scores well but covers the mines, not the rock.

alignments.label: Black fuel from the earth

britannica.quote: a black inflammable fossil, dug out of the earth in beds or seams

wikipedia.quote: a combustible black or brownish-black sedimentary rock, formed as rock strata called coal seams

alignments.note: A change in language. In 1797 a fossil was anything dug out of the earth, and inflammable now reads as combustible.

alignments.label: Hardened mineral bitumen

britannica.quote: Some hold it to be a mineral bitumen

wikipedia.quote: dead plant matter decays into peat

alignments.note: A change in knowledge. Coal is not a mineral liquid that hardened. It is the remains of plants.

alignments.label: Made from buried plants

britannica.quote: others think it is formed of trees and other vegetables, buried in the earth and changed by length of time

wikipedia.quote: converted into coal by the heat and pressure of deep burial over millions of years

alignments.note: The second 1797 opinion holds. Wikipedia adds heat and pressure, and gives the time as millions of years.

alignments.label: Fern impressions in shale

britannica.quote: the slate or shale which lies above the coal often bears the impressions of ferns and other plants

wikipedia.quote: Fossils of plants, such as ferns and giant club mosses, are common in the shale beds

alignments.note: The same observation in both texts. The 1797 entry used it as evidence for a plant origin, which was the right conclusion.

alignments.label: Laid down by the deluge

britannica.quote: supposed by many to have been laid down by the waters of the deluge

wikipedia.quote: wetland forests that grew during the Carboniferous and Permian periods, hundreds of millions of years ago

alignments.note: A change in knowledge. The plants grew and died where the coal is now, over a very long time, not in one flood.

alignments.label: An inexhaustible stock

britannica.quote: the stock is so great that it may be thought inexhaustible

wikipedia.quote: British coal output reached its peak in 1913 and then declined

alignments.note: Output fell for a century after 1913. Inference: cost and policy closed the mines as well as the loss of easy seams, but the stock did not prove endless.

alignments.label: Fire-damp explodes

britannica.quote: an inflammable vapour called fire-damp, which, taking fire from their candles, explodes with great violence

wikipedia.quote: Firedamp, a gas that is mostly methane, collects in coal mines and can explode when it meets a flame

alignments.note: The danger is the same. Wikipedia names the gas: methane.

alignments.label: Coke for smelting iron

britannica.quote: what remains is called coke, which is now used for smelting iron

wikipedia.quote: Coke, made by heating coal without air, is used to smelt iron ore in blast furnaces

alignments.note: The use of coke for iron was new in 1797 and still holds. Both texts also name coal tar.

alignments.label: Coal and climate

wikipedia.quote: Coal is the largest single source of the carbon dioxide emissions that cause climate change

alignments.note: New knowledge. The 1797 entry treats burning coal only as a benefit.

suggestedQuestions: What did the 1797 entry say about the origin of coal?
Was the 1797 entry right about fire-damp?
Did the 1797 entry think British coal would run out?

What did the 1797 entry say about the or.answer: It gave two opinions: a mineral bitumen that hardened in the earth, or trees and plants changed by time [B2]. It used fern impressions in the shale as evidence for plants [B3]. Wikipedia confirms the plant origin: peat buried and changed by heat and pressure over millions of years [W2]. The 1797 idea that the deluge laid down the beds [B4] is wrong; the plants grew in ancient wetland forests [W3].

Was the 1797 entry right about fire-damp.answer: Yes. It described an inflammable vapour that takes fire from candles and kills miners [B6]. Wikipedia describes the same danger and names the gas as mostly methane [W6].

Did the 1797 entry think British coal wo.answer: No. It said the stock in Britain might be thought inexhaustible [B5]. Wikipedia says British output peaked in 1913 and then declined, and most mines are now closed [W5].
